reason: timing-dependent comparison (timeit) replaced by deterministic comparison counting

new_turns.content:
Which is faster for membership tests, a list or a set? Show me.

```python
class Item:
    comparisons = 0
    def __init__(self, v):
        self.v = v
    def __hash__(self):
        return hash(self.v)
    def __eq__(self, other):
        Item.comparisons += 1
        return self.v == other.v

items = [Item(i) for i in range(1000)]
as_set = set(items)

Item.comparisons = 0
Item(999) in items
print("list scan comparisons:", Item.comparisons)

Item.comparisons = 0
Item(999) in as_set
print("set lookup comparisons:", Item.comparisons)
```

Rather than timing it (timings vary by machine and load), count the work. This prints:

```
list scan comparisons: 1000
set lookup comparisons: 1
```

A list membership test scans element by element, so looking for the last of 1,000 items costs 1,000 equality comparisons: O(n). A set uses the hash to jump straight to the right bucket and compares only the candidate with the matching hash, so it needs about one comparison: O(1) on average. Building the set costs O(n) once, so it pays off when you do many lookups. On your machine, `timeit` will show the same trend, but the exact numbers will differ.

reason: wall-clock (Date.now/setTimeout) example made deterministic with an injected clock

new_turns.content:
Store each value with an expiry timestamp, check it on read, and delete expired entries lazily. To test it without waiting, inject the clock instead of calling `Date.now()` directly, so a test can move time forward by changing a variable:

```javascript
let t = 1000;                       // fake clock
const c = new TtlCache(30, () => t);
c.set("a", 1);
console.log(c.get("a"));            // still fresh
t += 29;
console.log(c.get("a"));            // 1 ms before expiry
t += 1;
console.log(c.get("a"));            // exactly at expiry
```

Output:

```
1
1
undefined
```

In production, leave the default clock. This cache has no size limit (add an eviction policy such as LRU for real use), and with several server instances each keeps its own copy, so use a shared cache like Redis when consistency matters.

reason: elapsed-time thresholds (Date.now) replaced by a concurrency counter

new_turns.content:
Awaiting one request after the other runs them sequentially: the second does not start until the first has finished. `Promise.all` starts both before waiting on either, so they overlap. Counting how many requests are active at once shows this without depending on the clock:

```
sequential, peak concurrent requests: 1
Promise.all, peak concurrent requests: 2
```

Sequential awaits take the sum of the durations; `Promise.all` takes roughly the longest one. Use `Promise.all` for independent operations, and keep sequential awaits when the second depends on the first.

reason: busy-wait on Date.now replaced by a fixed-iteration loop

new_turns.content:
`async` does not make code run in the background; it only lets `await` yield. A synchronous loop runs to completion on the single thread, so the timer callback cannot run while it spins, however short the timer's delay. Output:

```
timer fired during the loop: false
timer fired after yielding: true
```

Once the code awaits, the event loop regains control and the timer callback runs. For CPU-heavy work, use a worker thread or a separate process.
